title: The Burton Trial
note: Salt Lake Herald, February 21 – March 6, 1879. “The Burton Trial,” daily reports of Burton’s trial for the murder of Isabella Bowman. The fullest account in the free archives. Former Morrisites testified for the prosecution and gave their homes in 1879. Among them were James Bowman (of Soda Springs since 1863), Mrs. Mary Anderson (of Soda Springs), Caroline Eliason, Mrs. Emma Just (of the Snake River valley, Oneida County, Idaho), Jacob Johnson, Thomas Williams (of Ogden since 1865), Philip Hewitt (Salt Lake City) and a man from Hyrum whose name the scan garbles. Men of the posse also took the stand, among them Christopher Sproat, William H. Hunt and Dan Camomile. The defense called Thomas Abbott of Farmington, Robert W. Burton of Kaysville, John C. Thompson of Riverdale and Burton himself. Abraham Taylor, one of the seven convicted in 1863, testified near the close (reported March 4). The text of these scans is poor, and the names are as read from it. title: Railroad Meeting at Gwendale
note: New North-West, April 16, 1875, p. 2. “Railroad Meeting at Gwendale.” Also June 18, 1875, p. 3; September 8, 1876, p. 3; July 6, 1877, p. 3; August 31, 1877, p. 3; April 30, 1880, p. 4; January 20, 1882, p. 3; March 10, 1882, p. 3; May 4, 1883, p. 3. Notices that place Gwendale, later Morristown, in the upper Deer Lodge valley. The April 1875 mass meeting of “the citizens of Upper Deer Lodge Valley” at the Gwendale school house was chaired by Morgan Evans, with W. Watkin Thomas on the resolutions committee. Primaries were held at Wier’s store (1875); the 1876 election judges for Gwendale were Morgan Evans, Peter Jessen and Wm Wier; a W W Thomas of Gwendale paid a subscription (1877); and a fifty-ton smelter at Gwendale began work in August 1877. A land-office notice of March 1880 lists Warm Springs settlers whose homestead claims awaited a hearing on whether the land was mineral, among them Daniel James, William P. Thomas, Morgan Evans and Peter Jessen. In January 1882 John R. Eardley built a store at “Daniel James’ corner, Warm Springs settlement,” and in March he was appointed postmaster “at Willow Glen on Warm Spring creek, where the Gwendale postoffice formerly was.” By 1883 school district No. 6 was called Willow Glen. None of these items calls anyone a Morrisite. note: Helena Weekly Herald, April 22, 1880, p. 7. “A Little Girl Burned to Death.” Reprints the New North-West’s account of the death of the five-year-old daughter of Andrew Hendrickson, later president of the Montana Morrisites, at the family’s farm a few miles from Deer Lodge: her clothes caught fire from burning rubbish in the yard, and she lived twelve hours. In England George Williams heard of it within weeks: on June 21, 1880, he wrote to William James of the “general mourning & sorrow” the news had cast and sent his sympathy to the Hendricksons (Church History Library, MS 31876). title: [Untitled item], New North-West
note: New North-West, September 3, 1886, p. 3. Also February 19 and March 26, 1886, p. 3. “A Mormon Church, of the Morrisite branch, we are informed, is being constructed under the superintendence of Elder Clapp on the Cottonwood road about a half mile east of town.” An Elder J. C. Clapp had preached at the Deer Lodge court house in February and March 1886, once on the “Origin of the American Indians,” a Book of Mormon theme. The Morrisites’ own minutes settle the question: in November 1886 their council recorded an invitation from “Elder Clapp of the Reorganized Church” to use that church’s meeting house at Deer Lodge City while he was preaching in Utah (Church History Library, MS 32226, minutebook, pp. 37–38). The building was the Reorganized Church’s, not a Morrisite church; Clapp was very probably the RLDS missionary Joseph C. Clapp. Other links: Chronicling America: https://www.loc.gov/resource/sn84038125/1886-02-19/ed-1/?sp=3; Chronicling America: https://www.loc.gov/resource/sn84038125/1886-03-26/ed-1/?sp=3 Listed on https://morrisite.org/newspapers.html#np-1891

title: From Morrisites to Marcus Daly
note: Montana Standard (Butte), July 2, 1989, pp. 69–71. Roger Kelley, “From Morrisites to Marcus Daly.” An interview with the Anaconda historian Alice Finnegan. She calls the Morrisites the area’s first settlers, says they wintered at Gregson (now Fairmont Hot Springs) before homesteading, and names Morgan Evans, who bought the land for Daly’s town and smelter, as a Morrisite. Morris’s Anaconda, Montana (1997) describes Evans’s arrival in 1866 without calling him one, and he is not on the 1861–62 roll; the claim is unconfirmed.
